title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

reading.body:
This is an impersonation carried out with synthetic video. A generated video appeared to feature a well known financial sector personality and promoted an investment with claimed significant returns. The failure sits at the point of first contact, where a fabricated likeness was accepted as a real endorsement, and nothing in the chain that followed required the fraudsters to prove who they were.

The rest of the fraud ran through ordinary channels rather than through the video itself. Contact moved to WhatsApp, the victim was urged to pay more after a small initial payment and was encouraged to borrow money, opened several online accounts, and gave the fraudsters remote access to a computer, with funds going to accounts controlled by criminals. Catching it at the video stage would have taken independent confirmation that the person shown had actually made the endorsement and that the provider was authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, the two checks the police pointed to.

What is not established is who the figure was, whether that person knew of or took part in the fraud, and whether any arrest, charge or conviction has followed. The account of the loss and the method comes from the Police Service of Northern Ireland.

reports.title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

summary:
A person in Ards and north Down lost £250,000 to an AI scam, the Police Service of Northern Ireland said. The victim saw an AI generated video that appeared to feature a well known financial sector personality. It promoted an investment with claimed significant returns. After a small initial payment, the victim was contacted on WhatsApp and urged to pay more. The fraudsters had the victim open several online accounts and gained remote access to their computer, claiming to help with the investment. Police called it a sophisticated and substantial fraud.

The PSNI did not name the celebrity. BBC News NI has seen similar scams using financial experts such as Martin Lewis, Peter Jones and Steven Bartlett. Police said the victim was encouraged to borrow money, and funds went to accounts controlled by criminals. Superintendent Joanne Gibson, who chairs the Scamwise Partnership, urged people to stop and check financial activity and to talk to relatives about fraud. Police advised independently verifying who they deal with and checking that financial services providers are authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority.
